voices.1: en-US-AvaMultilingualNeural (chosen voice), base rate -8%, directed per passage (render_edge.py)

tracks.room: The Pla de la Seu · on the square in front of the cathedral, to one side of the steps (heard before you go in)
tracks.title: Welcome to Barcelona Cathedral
tracks.where: On the Pla de la Seu, the open square in front of the cathedral, standing to one side of the steps up to the main door so the way stays clear; heard before you go in.
tracks.what: Not the Sagrada Família: a basilica dedicated by Benedict XVI on 7 Nov 2010 (F16.5 OK, S37); this is the cathedral of the Holy Cross and Saint Eulàlia, la Seu (F7.1 OK M1, F16.1 OK, §19); "more than seventeen hundred years of history" (F1.18 OK, O6); the route in one breath, version-neutral (PLAN §1 route, Variant A, O1); practical lines once: headphones / working church (ROUTE §1.5), hat off and voice low (F17.6 DATED, A2), no photos during services (F17.7 OFF, O7), small lift so a wait (no capacity, no times; COMP §2.2), offline (COMP §4.2-2); lengths per lead's decision 1 and the route audit R5 (Full ≈ 95–97 with a 5-min lift wait: "a little more with a wait for the lift"). No Gaudí, no UNESCO, no left/right, no date but 2010.
tracks.listen: A warm welcome that clears up the Sagrada Família mix-up, says what this building is, and sets out the walk and the few practical things.

tracks.room: The Pla de la Seu · at the end of the square by the two Roman towers, the cathedral in view
tracks.title: The Pla de la Seu — The bishops never moved
tracks.where: At the end of the square where two old stone towers stand, close to them but clear of the crowd, turned back so the cathedral front is in view.
tracks.what: Roman Barcino, 10 BC under Augustus, "a small fortified city covering just ten hectares" (F1.1, F1.2 OK, A1); two walls, 1st and 3rd century (F1.3 OK, A1; not said which these towers are); the decumanus gate at Plaça Nova (G120 OK, GA4; "round" not used); the first official see in the corner of the walled town (F1.4 OK, A1, S6); the first church under the cathedral, never dug (F1.5 HEDGE, S6); the dedication to the Holy Cross in 599 (F1.14 OK, O1); Almanzor's raid of 985, about a hundred documents saved (F1.16 OK, O9); Brossa's Barcino letters where the aqueduct reached the city (F6.9 OK A11, G121 OK GS22; no date; O13). Praetextatus 343 (F1.13) left out for the date count.
tracks.listen: How a ten-hectare Roman town put its first church in this corner, and why the bishops have never left it.

tracks.room: The Pla de la Seu · with the Casa de l'Ardiaca in view, beside the cathedral
tracks.title: The Pla de la Seu — A square from after the war
tracks.where: On the square, turned towards the old stone house built against the Roman wall beside the cathedral, with its door in view; stay clear of the steps.
tracks.what: The square opened after the Civil War, avenue 1939–1958 (F6.1 HEDGE, safe wording "after the war, over almost twenty years"; A6, S23); the Barri de la Catedral "one of the most affected", Sant Felip Neri 30 Jan 1938, 42 dead incl. 20 children (G112 OK, GS20; no direction; never "the cathedral was hit"); the Casa de l'Ardiaca built around the 12th century "taking advantage of part of Barcelona's old Roman wall" (F6.3 OK, A6); rebuilt by Lluís Desplà, Gothic "with some Renaissance features" (F6.4 OK, A6); forward to 034 (safe); Picasso's friezes on the College of Architects, drawings ready Oct 1960, sandblasted by Carl Nesjar, the dust paraphrased (F6.8 OK, A12). Letterbox (G124) left out: conditional on O13 and over the aim.
tracks.listen: Why the open square in front of the cathedral is younger than it looks, and the house that moved into the Roman wall.

tracks.room: The facade · on the square, far enough back to see the whole front
tracks.title: The facade — Drawn in 1408, built in 1887
tracks.where: On the square facing the cathedral, far enough back to see the whole front from the door up to the spires and the lantern tower behind it.
tracks.what: Neo-Gothic front, "following 15th-century plans" (F5.23 OK, M1); Carlí of Rouen's 1408 portal design, ink on twelve parchments of which four are lost, 3.11 m tall, in the archive, not on show (F5.1, F5.3 OK, S7, A7, S25); front closed with a plain wall in 1417, said as "nine years later" (F3.20 OK, O1, S7); lack of budget (Q13, F5.4 OK, S25); the 1882 competition rule, said as "in the 1880s" (F5.5 OK, A7); Manuel Girona, banker and former mayor, failed to raise the money and paid (F5.9, F5.10 OK; wording per COAC re-read, see notes); begun summer 1887, finished 12 Feb 1890 on her feast day (F5.12, F5.13 OK, S24, S7); lantern tower finished 1913 by his children (F5.16 HEDGE: 1913 only; O1); version-neutral Gaudí sentence (F5.7, F18.5); look: Christ on the central pillar, apostles either side (F5.21 OK, S24), the sober sides (F5.25 OK, M1). Agapit Vallmitjana (optional) left out.
tracks.listen: The front you photograph was drawn in 1408 and built almost five centuries later, when a banker finally paid for it.

tracks.room: The facade · same spot
tracks.title: The facade — The design that lost
tracks.where: Same spot on the square, facing the front, far enough back to see the lantern tower rising behind it.
tracks.what: Joan Martorell's rejected entry, with popular and press support, turned down by the Royal Academy of San Fernando on "rather weak grounds" (F5.6 OK, S24, S25, A7); helped by the very young Lluís Domènech i Montaner and Antoni Gaudí, "drafted by Antoni Gaudí" (F5.7 OK, A7, S25); the winner under Josep Oriol Mestres's name, the paymaster's hand in it (F5.8 HEDGE, safe wording); critics: the lantern tower borrowed from the loser (F5.20 OK, S24, S25); Mestres died and August Font took over (F5.14 OK, S24, optional, used). Girona's marquisate (F5.11) left out: not re-read. No dates (004 has them).
tracks.listen: Gaudí did work on this facade, on paper, for the design that lost, and the winners were accused of borrowing from it.

tracks.room: Inside the main door · just inside, to one side, looking along the nave to the choir screen
tracks.title: Inside the main door — A tower over the door
tracks.where: Just inside the main door, a step to one side so people can come in, looking along the nave towards the marble screen of the choir.
tracks.what: The cimbori over the entrance, unusual (F4.9 OK, S7, O4), 41 m inside (F5.18 OK, O4; see notes on "high"); Gual and the carpenter Aigüents's eighteen-day trip to Valencia in 1421, the provisional roof until the early 20th century (F3.14 OK, S7; "almost five hundred years" our arithmetic, no 1913 here); the bay by the facade the longest, to carry it (F4.8 OK, O4); three aisles, one apse and ambulatory (F4.1 OK, O4); side aisles almost as high (F4.2 HEDGE wording), 26 m centre (F4.3 OK, O4); over 150 years without interrupting the services (F3.4 HEDGE wording, A4); begun behind the altar towards the door (F3.8 OK); 215 keystones found painted in the 1970 restoration (F4.10 OK, O4). Pere Joan's keystone (F4.11) left out until O15.
tracks.listen: Why Barcelona's lantern tower stands over the door instead of the altar, and the stopgap roof that sat on it for almost five hundred years.

tracks.room: The Lepanto chapel · at its doorway, outside; never inside during a service
tracks.title: The Lepanto chapel — The Christ older than its battle
tracks.where: At the doorway of the chapel of the Christ of Lepanto, close to the main door on the right as you face the high altar; stay outside the doorway, to one side, and never go in during a service.
tracks.what: "The most venerated image in Barcelona" (F10.4 OK, O8); the chapel named once (ROUTE §0.2): the Christ of Lepanto chapel, the chapel of the Blessed Sacrament; tradition: aboard the flagship at Lepanto, 1571 (F10.5 LEGEND, O8; Don John from S15), dodged a Turkish cannonball (F10.6 LEGEND, O8; the hull tradition F10.7, optional, cut for length); the cannonball story in the confraternity's statutes of 1762, the earliest written telling the historian cites (F10.6, S15 p. 28; see notes), no archival document of 1571 (F10.9 OK, S15 p. 24), Hanß "it cannot be proven…" (Q7, S15 p. 27); "not from the 16th century, as was believed" (Q6, F10.8, O8; no century of ours); darkness from smoke and candle wax, later varnishes; restored because the paint was flaking (F10.10, O8, wording per re-read); the room built by Arnau Bargués in 1407, chapter house until the 1670s (F10.1, F10.2 OK, O7, O11); not the Chapter Hall museum (Conventions); E-safe clause on Oleguer (F10.19, O11); "Most of the year … In Lent, it's moved" (F10.12 OK/DATED, O8). Confraternity 1651 (F10.11) left out for the date count.
tracks.listen: The crucifix that tradition sends into the Battle of Lepanto, and the evidence that it was already old when the battle was fought.

tracks.room: The Lepanto chapel · at its doorway, outside
tracks.title: The Lepanto chapel · Extra · The bishop under the crucifix
tracks.where: Same place, at the doorway of the chapel of the Christ of Lepanto, outside it and to one side; never go in during a service.
tracks.what: Sant Oleguer, bishop of Barcelona from 1116, also archbishop of Tarragona after its conquest, died 6 March 1137, canonised 1675 (F10.16, F10.17 OK, O10, O11; never 1676); his tomb under the crucifix (O11); Baroque tomb, medieval figure by Pere Sanglada, 1406, the only one of his surviving works in alabaster, kept when the new tomb was made in 1675 (F10.19, F10.20 OK, O10, S9); the correction, forward to 022 (safe): marble in the crypt; body in bishop's robes in a glass case in a chamber, shown on 6 March (F10.18 OK/DATED, O10; no hours, "his body", never a miracle claim); next door, Sança Ximenis de Cabrera's chapel of 1431 and the alabaster tomb argued to be her mother's (G37 OK, G38 HEDGE, GS9; ONLY if O4/O5 find it in view, else cut the paragraph). 1701 procession and the Pentecost keystone (optional) left out.
tracks.listen: The bishop-saint who lies under the crucifix, the alabaster everyone confuses with Santa Eulàlia's tomb, and a noblewoman's tomb next door that may be her mother's.

tracks.room: The choir screen · a few steps back from the white marble screen at the end of the choir, facing it
tracks.title: The choir screen — The sculptor who never came back
tracks.where: In the nave, a few steps back from the white marble screen that closes the end of the choir, facing it, with its central door and the carved panels either side in view.
tracks.what: The trascor, the choir screen, begun by Bartolomé Ordóñez, in Barcelona from May 1517 (F9.28 OK, S12, O4); four scenes of Santa Eulàlia's martyrdom, two each side of the door (ROUTE S5 OFF; O24); very low relief praised for its delicacy and its details, the flames (F9.29, S12; "schiacciato" not spoken); inventory of 15 Oct 1519: two large finished Eulàlia panels and two finished statues, one of Eulàlia (F9.29 OK, S12; the second statue's saint not named, see notes); he went to Carrara, "quondam" in a 1521 payment (F9.30 OK, S12); others finished it, among them Pedro Villar (F9.28, O4); honest aside on which two (F9.29); forward to 022 (safe). No death place or cause; no quarry.
tracks.listen: A Renaissance sculptor began this marble screen of Santa Eulàlia, left for Carrara, and never came back.

tracks.room: The baptistery · at the chapel's entrance, the font and its tall window in view
tracks.title: The baptistery — Baptised here
tracks.where: At the entrance of the first chapel on the left as you face the high altar, beside the main door, with the font and the tall stained-glass window in view; stand aside if worshippers are there.
tracks.what: The early baptistery found in 1968 under the cathedral (F1.7 OK, A1, S6), later rebuilt as an eight-sided pool (F1.8 safe wording, S6); not visible, never "go and see"; the window of Saint Michael and Noli me tangere, Gil de Fontanet, 1495, from a design by Bartolomé Bermejo, in place, "the most important of all the Cathedral windows" (F4.14 OK, O4; scene not described before O14); forward to 034 (safe); Antoni Canet's carved stone washing cupboard (levador) of 1406, his first surviving work, the vault closed c. 1420, on corbels as heads: a girl with a low neckline and a necklace, a hooded man with a full beard (G44 OK, GS10; O14); "a 15th-century font" (F10.28 HEDGE, S34; no maker, no 1433); the plaque of April 1493 and its doubtful date (F10.29 HEDGE, S34; ONLY if O14 finds the plaque, else cut that paragraph).
tracks.listen: The chapel where the cathedral baptises, with a window designed by a great painter, two stone faces to find, and a plaque about Columbus with a doubtful date.

tracks.room: The Sant Iu door · inside, near the side door, the organ in the gallery above
tracks.title: The Sant Iu door — A Saracen under the organ
tracks.where: Inside the church, near the Sant Iu side door towards the far end of the left aisle as you face the high altar, the great organ in its gallery high above the door; stand out of the way of the door and the lift chapel beside it.
tracks.what: The carassa, a carved Saracen's head under the organ, the cathedral's from the 16th century (F11.22 OK, A5); eyes and mouth moved on St Stephen's, Holy Innocents' and New Year's Eve, strings from inside the organ, beard remade in 1892 from three donkey tails (G116 HEDGE, GS21, attributed to "a newspaper"); the sweets told of Barcelona's carasses in general (Q9, A5; G117: the press puts the sweets at another church); taken down by the mid-20th century for the noise and because the head was seen "as an apology for xenophobia and racism" (F11.23 OK, A5; "Moor" not used); the 1988 Christmas-fair carassa (F11.23, optional) cut for length; past tense for the head (O18; museum not mentioned); the organ, organbuilders Pere Flamenc and Antoni Carbonell, contract 1538, said "around 1540" (F11.17 OK, F11.18 HEDGE, S21); 57 stops, four keyboards and pedal, Blancafort 1985 and 1994 (F11.20 OK, O6); "the largest and most important historical organ in Catalonia" (F11.19, S21, attributed to its restorers); forward: Carbonell in the choir for the Golden Fleece (S12 n. 87; safe 018); the 1298 inscription outside, paraphrased, no "go and look" (F3.1, F3.2 OK, S7, O1; Q2 not quoted). Audit fixes, 14 Nov 2026: cut after the audits: the workshop's superlative and the payoff; Carbonell's link to the choir now as 'a joiner of the same name' (facts S4); see notes/AUDIT_FIXES.md.
tracks.listen: A carved head under the organ that rolled its eyes at Christmas, why the city took such heads down, and the great organ above them.

tracks.room: The lift · in the queue at the chapel of the Holy Innocents, or at the top beside the lift
tracks.title: The lift — Eulàlia strikes the hours
tracks.where: In the queue for the roof lift at the chapel of the Holy Innocents, beside the Sant Iu door; with no queue, at the top, standing to one side of the lift. Nothing needs to be seen.
tracks.what: The hour bell Eulàlia and the quarter bell Honorata, both cast by Francesc Calbetó in 1865, Eulàlia in the tower over the Sant Iu door (F11.8 OK, G59, S17; O6 confirms Eulàlia in the Sant Iu tower); the "rebellious" Honorata "imprisoned" and melted down by Philip V in 1714, as the city tells it (F11.7 HEDGE, A4), and the bell survey's silence (G58, S17); two eight-sided towers over fifty metres, over the Sant Iu door with the clock and over the cloister door (F11.1 HEDGE wording, F11.2 OK), built after the Romanesque tower came down around 1380, first bell hoisted 1393 (F11.3, F11.5, S7: year not spoken), one medieval, its twin finished two centuries later (F11.4 OK); l'Esquella de Prima, 1321 (F11.6 OK); about twenty bells, nearly all with women saints' names (F11.12 HEDGE wording); eleven in the cloister tower, the Crown of Aragon pattern (F11.11 OK, G63 OK); "the thief's bell", unexplained (G62); la Tomasa for the noon Angelus (F11.13 OK DATED); the 1865 clock regulated by electric impulses (G60 OK, optional, used). Audit fixes, 14 Nov 2026: cut after the audits: the clock line and 'If you're here at noon'; the 1321 bell no longer 'older than the crypt'; see notes/AUDIT_FIXES.md.
tracks.listen: The voice of the old town's clock, a bell the city says a king punished, and the twenty-odd named bells in the two towers.

tracks.room: The lift · same place (queue or top)
tracks.title: The lift — Lightning and firecrackers
tracks.where: Same place as the last stop: in the lift queue at the chapel of the Holy Innocents, beside the Sant Iu door, or at the top to one side of the lift. Nothing needs to be seen.
tracks.what: Lightning on 5 April 1582 and 27 August 1646 (F4.18 OK SEC, S32 p. 56; second date spoken as "sixty-four years later", our arithmetic); the Saint John's Eve firecrackers of 1606 (F4.19 HEDGE, one press source, S30, attributed); the roof reopened in 2024 after works: 2,002 m² of ceramics, new stairs, handrails, an updated lift, the original floor tiles recovered, paid by the Catalan and Spanish governments (F15.13 DATED, S35; O6; no sums); gargoyles: Joan Claperós made many for the cloister around 1450 (S33: "el 1450 realitzà nombroses gàrgoles", at the cloister), the city's count of two hundred and its bull, unicorn and elephant (F4.16 HEDGE, A4, attributed; 014 points only at what O7 sees). Audit fixes, 14 Nov 2026: the gargoyle animals stay as one attributed sentence, cut unless O7 finds one; see notes/AUDIT_FIXES.md.
tracks.listen: Storms, a midsummer near-miss and the newly renewed roof, told while you wait to go up.

tracks.room: The roof · on the terraces, the lantern tower over the main door in view
tracks.title: The roof — Saint Helena on the lantern
tracks.where: On the roof terraces, on the walkway, with the lantern tower over the main door in front of you and the statue on its top in view; keep to the walkway and out of the way of people passing.
tracks.what: Saint Helena with the Holy Cross on top of the cimbori, carved in 1910 by Eduard B. Alentorn (G54 OK OFF, GO2; F5.19; O6 "coronat per la imatge de Santa Helena sostenint la Santa Creu"); Helena, mother of Constantine, who found the True Cross as the story goes (GO2, told as "the story goes"); the cathedral of the Holy Cross (F7.1, G56); the facade's patrons, the Girona family, devoted to her, many bearing her name (GO2; spoken as "the family of the banker who paid for the front"); callback to the lantern you stood under (006, safe); around you: the two bell towers, one over the Sant Iu door with the clock, one over the cloister door (F11.2 OK; which is which from here: O7), the two side pinnacles, the cloister below (F17.5 OK, O6, O7 [OFF]); the Benedicció del Terme, every year in early May, from the cross on the apse roof (F11.28 OK OFF, O2; G55 OK OFF DATED, GO3); gargoyles without naming animals (F4.16 HEDGE, G65: none named until O7). Audit fixes, 14 Nov 2026: the towers now a callback to 012; the cloister line cut (015 is its home); 'Gothic' dropped from the pinnacles; see notes/AUDIT_FIXES.md.
tracks.listen: Why a woman with a cross stands on the lantern tower, and the cross at the far end from which the whole city is blessed once a year.

tracks.room: The roof · where the old town and the cloister are in view
tracks.title: The roof — The old town from above
tracks.where: On the terraces, at a spot on the walkway where you can see over the rooftops of the old town and down into the cloister garden.
tracks.what: Callback to the Roman corner and "the bishops never moved" (002, safe for E F; no re-telling); the cathedral's own list of its neighbours "a pocs metres": the Bishop's Palace, the Palau de la Generalitat, the City Hall, the Casa de l'Ardiaca (name and gloss only, E-safe), the Palau Reial Major, the Frederic Marès museum, the Archive of the Crown of Aragon (F17.5 OK OFF, O6; re-read: the PDF lists them as a few metres from the cathedral, not as seen from the roof, so the script claims nearness, not sightlines, until O7); the cloister below, its palms and the geese's pond (ROUTE S15, S17; F12.22 OK DATED; forward to 030, safe); the bookend on the horizon without its name (G64 HEDGE, GS13; lint bans the name outside 001; only if O7 ticks it, else cut the sentence). Audit fixes, 14 Nov 2026: the neighbours stay as a list; the look at them and the Sagrada Família line are separate cuttable sentences (O7); see notes/AUDIT_FIXES.md.
tracks.listen: The old town laid out around the bishops' corner, the cathedral's famous neighbours, and the cloister garden below.

tracks.room: The choir · inside, among the upper stalls (or at the entrance if closed)
tracks.title: The choir — Oak from Bruges
tracks.where: Inside the choir, the enclosure in the middle of the nave, standing where the tall upper row of seats is in view; if the choir is closed, at its entrance, looking in.
tracks.what: Q1 / F9.4 OK (S9, old CA, re-checked): the Llibre del cor, "Anglada fo tramès […] en Bruges per comprar fusta de roure a ops del demont dit cor" (spoken in English, "in old Catalan" once; never "rode", no route towns); the choir in the middle of the nave, in front of the crypt (F9.1 OK, S7); begun in the 1390s under Bishop Ramon d'Escales (F9.2 HEDGE wording; O7 1390, S9 1394); Sanglada directed the upper stalls 1394–1399, mainly Flemish oak, a team effort, formally finished 5 December 1399 (F9.3 OK, S9; "team effort" paraphrased); callback: Sanglada's alabaster figure of Sant Oleguer (008, safe in F; F10.19, F10.20); optional, used: the lower stalls won by Macià Bonafè against Joan Claperós (F9.7 OK, S10; year spoken as "half a century later"); look: the upper row's seat backs and armrests (O8).
tracks.listen: How a Barcelona sculptor went to Bruges for the oak of the canons' choir, and the team who carved it.

tracks.room: The choir · beside a seat with its folding ledge raised
tracks.title: The choir · Extra · Under the canons' seats
tracks.where: Inside the choir, beside one of the seats whose folding ledge is already raised, so the carving underneath shows; never lift a seat yourself.
tracks.what: The misericords under the canons' seats: daily life, music, dance, games, animals, monkeys aping people, a siren-bird holding a mirror, vanity (F9.5 OK, S9; "siren", never "mermaid"); the encyclopedia's words "detalls de la vida quotidiana, de treball i divertiment" (S9, CA, re-checked; spoken in English, "in Catalan" once); the stick-and-ball game the city speaks of (F9.6 HEDGE, A4; S9 also mentions a ball game; never the word the city uses), its "best test for the keen-eyed" (A4, attributed); look: the carving under the raised ledge, then one more along the row (O25).
tracks.listen: The everyday world the carvers hid under the canons' seats.

tracks.room: The choir · inside, where the painted shields above the upper stalls are in view (or at the entrance if closed)
tracks.title: The choir — Europe's most exclusive club
tracks.where: Inside the choir, standing where the row of painted coats of arms above the tall upper seats is in view; if the choir is closed, at its entrance, looking in.
tracks.what: Hook: the chapter of 5–8 March 1519 (G1 OK SEC, GS1; F9.16 OK; "most exclusive club" our gloss); version-neutral (H, E skip 016): the canons' choir in the middle of the church, the seats carved at the end of the 1300s (F9.1, F9.3); the Toisó d'Or founded in 1429 by Philip the Good, a duke, not a king, for prestige (F9.14 OK OFF, O5); Jason's fleece swapped by the chancellor for Gideon's (F9.15 OK OFF, Q5 paraphrase, no quotation marks; "two years later" = 1431); the young King Charles, grand master, held its chapter here; the first outside Burgundian territory and the only general chapter in Spain, "as far as we know" (F9.16, F18.39 wording; F9.17, G10, G128; S27); fifty-one coats of arms, one per knight, about a dozen present (G7, G6 OK SEC, GS1; our juxtaposition); Charles had enlarged the order and the new places were filled here (G8 safe wording; S27, GS2); lead's decision 5: no king named until O8 finds Louis II's shield, so "the arms of distant kings"; painted for the chapter of 1519 by Joan de Borgonya, a northern painter living in Barcelona (G13 HEDGE, F9.19 HEDGE wording; GS1, GS3); the order's treasurers paid, not the chapter (F9.20 OK, S12 pp. 142–143); payoff (F9.26 OK, S12 p. 142).
tracks.listen: How the knights of the Golden Fleece met in these seats in March 1519, and why fifty-one shields hang over a dozen knights.

tracks.room: The choir · same place, among the shields (or at the entrance if closed)
tracks.title: The choir — Four days in March
tracks.where: Same place as the last stop, inside the choir with the painted shields above the upper seats in view; if the choir is closed, at its entrance.
tracks.what: 5 March 1519, about three in the afternoon, the procession for the vespers of Saint Andrew, the order's patron, with trumpets, clarions, sackbuts and shawms (G3 OK SEC, GS1 p. 169; never "scarlet"); the 1519 relation quoted in Spanish: "y luego los cantores de la capilla, y el gran órgano, cantaron muy solemnemente vísperas y completas" (G4 OK SEC, GS1 p. 169; "in Spanish" once); not today's organ, which came about twenty years later (G4 note, F11.17–F11.18; callback 011, safe in F); the days: patron saint, the dead brothers with a Requiem, a Mass of Our Lady on the last morning, 8 March (G5 OK, GS1 p. 168 and n. 24); the Gideon tapestries brought for the ceremony, which changed the choir's sound (G11 OK SEC, GS1 p. 170; never "from Flanders"; callback 018, Gideon); the knights seated with their arms in the painted stalls (G12 OK, GS1 p. 170); Maximilian's exequies, 2 March 1519 a day of them, catafalque, the royal chapel's platform by the door of the high altar, trumpets silent, bells twice a day (G14 OK SEC, GS1 pp. 164–167, 173; F9.25; never "hung in black", no death date); the news of the imperial election, 6 July 1519, while Charles was in Barcelona (G16 OK SEC, S11 p. 268; spoken "that July").
tracks.listen: The four days of the knights' chapter in sound: trumpets, singers, tapestries, a funeral before it and the news that came after.

tracks.room: The choir · at its entrance, the pulpit beside you, the spires over the stalls in view
tracks.title: The choir — A canopy of spires
tracks.where: At the choir's entrance, beside the wooden pulpit, where you can look up at the carved spires over the upper seats.
tracks.what: Michael Lochner, a carver of German origin, in Barcelona by 1483, workshop in Carrer de Mercaders, died in Barcelona in June 1490 (F9.8 OK, S8, S10; spoken "seven years later"); the spires over the upper stalls begun in 1483, "probablement projectats en època del mestre Pere Sanglada" (F9.9 OK, S8); his assistant Joan Frederic, also German, carried on and finished the first phase in 1497 (S10 "va acabar la primera fase"; S8 "quedà interromput de nou": so "the first phase", not "finished"); three generations: Sanglada's team, Bonafè, Lochner and Frederic (F18.25 correction; callback 016, safe in F); the pulpit, by Sanglada, around 1400 (F9.11 HEDGE wording: 1394–96, paid in full 1403), six faces, fifteen full-length figures, painted by Lluís Borrassà (S9); optional, cut for length: the Annunciation crowning its stair, attributed to Jordi de Déu, perhaps with Sanglada (F9.12 HEDGE, S9 re-read: not on the pulpit itself but on the stair); the 14th-century bishop's chair presiding over the choir (F9.13 OK, S1; no look until O8 places it); O7's "at the entrance to the choir on the right is the wooden pulpit" (OFF) used for the place, not for left or right.
tracks.listen: The German carver who crowned the stalls with spires a century late, and the pulpit at the choir's door.

tracks.room: The crypt · at the top of the stair down to the crypt, in front of the high altar
tracks.title: The crypt — Thirteen, according to tradition
tracks.where: At the top of the stair that goes down to the crypt, in front of the high altar, standing to one side so the steps stay clear.
tracks.what: Her name, "the well-spoken one" (F7.2 OK, A9); in the legend she answers Dacian with words and reason (A9); "according to tradition" a girl of thirteen from Sarrià who left her parents' home, persecution of 304, the governor Dacian (F7.3, O3, A9; never "the governor of Dacia", G79); thirteen tortures, one per year, as the story goes (F7.4 LEGEND, S18, A9); the oldest written account names three: the whips, the cross and fire (F7.7 OK as the passio, S5); crucified naked on an X-shaped cross (F7.5, A9); callback to the choir screen (009, safe in E F); optional barrel and street (F7.6 LEGEND, S18), cut for length; the turn: A9's "doubtful" and A10's "a single legend claimed by two different places" (F7.8 HEDGE, attributed; A10 now says more bluntly that everything suggests Barcelona's did not exist: not used, F18.24); a century ago Barcelona's historians doubted her (G66, GS14); the early-Christian cemetery under Santa Maria del Mar used to argue for an early cult (G67 HEDGE: "argue"); a 2023 study still treats it as open (G68, GS15); F7.8's two safe lines; the record: cult by the end of the 6th century, written story from the 7th (F7.9 OK, S5); co-patroness of the cathedral, the archdiocese and the city (F7.16 OK, O13; S18). Audit fixes, 14 Nov 2026: 'Barcelona has never had any doubt', 'naked' and the choir-screen callback cut (facts M1, route L7); see notes/AUDIT_FIXES.md.
tracks.listen: The legend of the girl of thirteen, told as a legend, and the honest question of whether she lived at all.

tracks.room: The crypt · down in the crypt with the tomb in view (or from the top of the stair)
tracks.title: The crypt — Two kings on the stairs
tracks.where: Down in the crypt, standing where you can see the marble tomb, out of the way of the steps; if the crypt is closed, at the top of its stair, with the tomb in view below.
tracks.what: Hook: July 1339, two kings and their queens, a cardinal and bishops (F8.5, F8.7 OK, S4; never "three queens"); Peter the Ceremonious's chronicle: he, the king of Mallorca, the cardinal, the archbishop and several bishops carried the body "with our own hands" (G75 OK SEC, GS15 pp. 121–122, a Spanish translation of the Catalan chronicle; spoken as reported speech, no quotation marks, until the Catalan is checked); version-neutral line (H skips 021); relics hidden, the story goes, when the Moors came (F7.11 HEDGE); found by Bishop Frodoí in 877 at Santa Maria de les Arenes, today Santa Maria del Mar (G70 OK, GS15 p. 120 "efectuada el 23 de octubre del año 877"; S5; never 878; the cathedral's saint page still says 878: not used); the correction, decision 6: white marble, partly painted and gilded (F8.8 OK, S4; O3 "polychromed marble"; G77 is the slip); look: the 1339 inscription round the friezes, naming the kings of Aragon and Mallorca (G73 OK, GS15 pp. 122, 126); the lid's front showing the 1339 transfer, "the king and four bishops" (F8.14, O3, S4); eight columns of different shapes (F8.16, S4); the keystone, the Virgin and Child crowning Eulàlia (F8.4 OK, O3, O4; "if you're down beside it"); behind it, only if visible, the 9th-century plaque, "Hic requiescit Beata Eulalia, martiris Christi, qui passa est in civitate Barchinona sub Daciano preside … et fuit inventa Frodoino episcopo …" (G72 OK, GS15 p. 119; F8.19; "in Latin" once; conditional); the masters: the crypt as Jaume Fabre's masterpiece, the tomb by the workshop of the Pisan Lupo di Francesco (F8.3, F8.9 OK, S4, S7, O3); betevé's "the most sacred place", paraphrased (F8.22 OK as opinion, S18); payoff. Not used: the Pope's visit (optional DATED, F7.19: left out to keep the dates to three); the 1343/1349 sequel (G127; PLAN §2 NOT still bars "within a few years Peter took Mallorca": lead to decide). Audit fixes, 14 Nov 2026: the kings' party listed once; the version-neutral line now 'by tradition a young girl martyred in 304' (route L1a: H keeps 'thirteen' in 030); the eight columns cut; see notes/AUDIT_FIXES.md.
tracks.listen: The day two kings carried Barcelona's saint into this crypt, and the marble tomb that records it.

tracks.room: The crypt · by the tomb, the reliefs on its box in view
tracks.title: The crypt — A comic strip in marble
tracks.where: Down in the crypt beside the marble tomb, out of the way of the steps, where the carved scenes on its box can be seen; if the crypt is closed, at the top of its stair.
tracks.what: Eight high reliefs following the Catalan versions of the Golden Legend (F8.13 OK, S4); the scenes as the cathedral describes them: talking with her parents, then walking alone; the trial, condemned by Dacian; death on the cross; the finger theft on the rear section (O3; COMP §1.2 says the reliefs are often hard to see, so the look is conditional); the finger legend (F7.14 LEGEND, O3, S18; "the story goes"); Lupo witnessing Jaume Fabre freeing a Greek slave, 1327 (F8.12 OK, S4; callback 022 Fabre, safe); the councillors' 1327 letter about the bishop's Pisan altar of 110 florins, mentioning "el mestre del sepulcre de Santa Eulàlia" (F8.11 OK, S4; paraphrased, no quotation marks); Not used (cut for length): the inscription's 287, "inexact" (G74 OK, GS15 p. 122); the four evangelists and the atlas in a lion skin (F8.17 OK, S4); the paymasters' heads on the arch (G85 HEDGE, press only: only if O10 finds them); the box c. 1327 / lid c. 1339 (F8.10, optional).
tracks.listen: Reading the saint's life off the marble box, and the two masters who made it, caught in one document.

tracks.room: Behind the high altar · in the ambulatory, the walkway behind the altar, the tall windows in view
tracks.title: Behind the high altar — They started at this end
tracks.where: In the ambulatory, the curving walkway behind the high altar, standing to one side of the flow where you can look up at the tall windows above its chapels.
tracks.what: The chevet, first phase: apse, ambulatory chapels, presbytery and crypt, mostly under Bishop Ponç de Gualba (F3.8, F3.21); the first master unnamed, Jaume Fabre hired 1317 from Mallorca, master for life (F3.6, F3.7, S7, A7); high altar consecrated "in the 1330s" (F3.9 safe wording); the oldest glass above the radial chapels, matching their saints, two with royal arms, the central window with the bishop's shield (F4.12, F4.13, G46, O4); Ponç de Gualba buried in the Patrocini chapel (G45, O17: no position given); DATED: twelve windows restored, finished 2024 (F4.15). Callback 022 (Fabre's crypt; safe in F). No 1298. Audit fixes, 14 Nov 2026: the 2024 windows line cut; Fabre's crypt hedged ('thought to be'); the crypt left out of the first-phase list (facts N15); 'the royal arms' (facts S5); see notes/AUDIT_FIXES.md.
tracks.listen: The cathedral began at this end, behind the altar: who built it, the oldest glass, and a bishop who lies under his own window.

tracks.room: Behind the high altar · in the ambulatory, by the chapel with Sant Ramon de Penyafort's tomb
tracks.title: Behind the high altar — The saint who sailed on his cloak
tracks.where: In the ambulatory, at the chapel whose sign names Sant Ramon de Penyafort, with his tomb in view; if no sign is found, anywhere along the walkway.
tracks.what: Sant Ramon de Penyafort: the Sóller voyage as legend (G49, GO1); died 1275 at Santa Caterina, canonised 1601 (spoken "more than three centuries later"), patron of Catalan lawyers, feast 7 January (G49 OK OFF); 1835: the convent's great fire and demolition 1836–37, the tomb moved to the cathedral (G50, GS12; F10.24; GO1); the Order of Mercy, 1218, "tradition says here" (F10.32 HEDGE; S31: 19 August 1218, the bishop of Barcelona, Pere Nolasc and thirteen knights, Penyafort advising, Jaume I helping, place not stated). Bishop not named (lint: Palou). Audit fixes, 14 Nov 2026: the lawyers and feast-day line cut; the 1835 order follows GO1 (facts S6); see notes/AUDIT_FIXES.md.
tracks.listen: A saint who, the story goes, sailed home on his cloak; why his tomb came here; and the order for ransoming captives that tradition says began in this cathedral.

tracks.room: The sacristy door · on the right of the high altar, below the two painted wooden coffins high on the wall
tracks.title: The sacristy door — The founders who were excommunicated
tracks.where: Beside the sacristy door, on the right of the high altar as you face it, standing back far enough to see two painted wooden coffins high on the wall.
tracks.what: The two painted wooden coffins on the sacristy wall, right of the high altar (G22, S19; G24, GS5); Almodis and Ramon Berenguer I married 1052, her two earlier husbands alive, his wife repudiated (F2.12, G28); al-Bakri's Tortosa fleet (G29 HEDGE, attributed); Ermessenda, Victor II, the excommunication, her later submission and request to lift it (G30); consecration of their cathedral, November 1058 (F2.3), "soon after"; MUHBA on the Gothic works destroying the Romanesque cathedral (Q12, F2.10, ES); Almodis killed by her stepson, 1071 (F2.13, G31); the move from probably Roman marble sarcophagi into painted wood, tradition vs "several other names" (F10.14, G23, G26); the 1603 Hercules belief (G25, as recorded); forward to the cloister door (028, safe F). Audit fixes, 14 Nov 2026: the Spanish quotation now paraphrased in English (the original stays in @sources); consecrated in the passive (facts M2); see notes/AUDIT_FIXES.md.
tracks.listen: The count and countess who built the cathedral before this one: a scandalous marriage, a pope's ban, a murder, and two painted boxes whose occupants are still argued over.

tracks.room: The cloister door · beside the white marble doorway, inside the church, the choir in view
tracks.title: The cloister door — The summer of 1936
tracks.where: Inside the church, beside the white marble doorway into the cloister, in the bay on the right of the high altar as you face it; stand out of the way of the door, with the choir in view across the church.
tracks.what: 1936: the cathedral "came through the summer of 1936 intact" (F15.7 HEDGE safe wording, M1); the Catalan government chose to safeguard it, the dean's words via Catalan News (F15.8 HEDGE, S16; no name); Sant Sever one of four churches in Ciutat Vella not burned, protected by the Mossos d'Esquadra (F15.9, S16); the lorry of Baroque carvings stopped in front of the cathedral and burned, "according to one account" (G109 HEDGE, GS19); the archive carried out in haste by Agustí Duran i Sanpere's service, back in spring 1939 (F15.10, G111, O9, CA); Sant Oleguer's tomb moved to the crypt (F10.22 OFF; callback 008, safe F); MNAC's conclusion that much of the interior survives (M1, attributed; its word "anarchists" not used). G114: protection still press + MNAC, hedge kept. Audit fixes, 14 Nov 2026: the Catalan quotation now paraphrased in English; see notes/AUDIT_FIXES.md.
tracks.listen: How the choir and the church around it came through July 1936 intact, while churches burned across the city, and how the archive was carried out and came home.

tracks.room: The cloister · just through the white marble door, facing back at it
tracks.title: The cloister — A door from the older cathedral
tracks.where: In the cloister, a few steps beyond the white marble door from the church, turned round to face it and its carved capitals.
tracks.what: The white marble cloister door: "Romanesque, made of white marble", "said to have come from the former Romanesque Cathedral" (F2.7 HEDGE, O7, EN); Italian white marble, five pointed archivolts, Job, the Annunciation, a warrior and a winged three-bodied dragon, late Romanesque of the full 13th century, its origin a hypothesis (S2, re-read); the garden's palms, magnolias, orange tree (F12.22 DATED); the 1078 sale and the canons' buildings and two cemeteries (F12.3, S2); chapels on three sides, the fourth with the Chapter Hall and Santa Llúcia (F12.23, G81); the second bell tower over this door, eleven bells (F11.2, F11.11, O6; callback 012). Callback 026 (the founders' church; safe F). Audit fixes, 14 Nov 2026: the garden and the bell-tower lines cut; see notes/AUDIT_FIXES.md.
tracks.listen: A white marble door that may come from the cathedral before this one, and the garden the canons lived and were buried around.

tracks.room: The cloister · beside the fountain pavilion, near the door from the church, its little vault overhead in view
tracks.title: The cloister — The egg the accountant wrote down
tracks.where: Beside the small vaulted pavilion over the fountain, in the corner of the cloister near the door from the church, where you can see up into its little vault.
tracks.what: L'ou com balla at Corpus, flowers and red cherries, the cathedral first in Barcelona, "at least to 1636" (F12.15, F12.16, F12.18, O2); the accounts recording eggs bought for Corpus and its octave (F12.16, A3); the egg popularly thought to be the Host (F12.19, A3 wording); the keystone of Saint George killing the dragon, the four evangelists seated on the ribs, the figure of Saint George on top (F12.10 corrected by S32 re-read, F12.12, M1); 1448 = the cloister's last vault, then the pavilion (F3.19, F12.9, S32); never consecrated, a Te Deum (F3.18, S2 re-read); the 1456 proclamation, old CA (Q4, F12.13, S32); Saint George's feasts held here (S32). Princess, Escuder and the keystone's day cut (see notes). Audit fixes, 14 Nov 2026: the old-Catalan quotation now paraphrased; 'first' attributed to the cathedral (facts S7); see notes/AUDIT_FIXES.md.
tracks.listen: How an accountant's entry for eggs dates Barcelona's dancing egg, why 1448 belongs to the cloister, and Saint George in the vault.

tracks.room: The cloister · on a walk with the pond in view (the far side if crowded)
tracks.title: The cloister — Thirteen geese
tracks.where: On a cloister walk with the geese's pond in view; if it's crowded by the pond, on the walk on the far side of the garden.
tracks.what: Thirteen white geese (F12.4 DATED, O2, O7); why thirteen: the cathedral's "according to tradition", her age at martyrdom (F12.5 LEGEND, O2); the city's "one for each of the agonies she suffered, as well as for the years of her life" (A4, EN); self-contained Eulàlia (version-neutral, H skips 021); documented since the 16th century (Q8, F12.6, O2); why geese: watchmen, purity, the goose-girl folk tale told as guesses (F12.7; G83 re-read: the goose-girl is the betevé article's own statement, not a canon's, so attributed to Barcelona's public television); their care (F12.8 DATED, O2).
tracks.listen: The cloister's famous geese: the tradition behind their number, the four centuries we can document, and the question nobody can answer.

tracks.room: The cloister · near the Pietat door, a carved capital in view
tracks.title: The cloister — A Bible on the capitals
tracks.where: In the cloister walk near the Pietat door, the door to the street with a Pietà carved above it, where a pillar's carved capital is also in view.
tracks.what: The twenty-one carved imposts on the pillars, Old Testament and the legend of the Holy Cross (F12.20, O7, S32), a stone Biblia pauperum promoted by Bishop Sapera (S32; "perhaps" for the reading); the Genesis capitals in front of the chapel of the Apostles attributed to Dello Delli, the chapel designed 1408 by Carlí (F12.21 HEDGE, G91, S33; callback 004 safe); the Pietat door, end of the 1300s, its Pietà attributed to Michael Lochner, canon Berenguer Vila kneeling, the original in the cathedral museum (F12.26 HEDGE, S7, S8, S33; callback 020 safe); the chapels first dedicated to guilds' and institutions' saints (ROUTE S15 OFF); the shoemakers' Sant Marc chapel and Bernat Martorell's altarpiece, 1437 (F10.25, G35; no location); Martorell's grave under the cloister (G48; no slab). No guild slabs (F12.25, G90: O19).
tracks.listen: A picture Bible carved on the cloister's pillars, a German carver's Pietà over the street door, and a guild that hired the city's leading painter.

tracks.room: The cloister · at the doorway of the chapel of Santa Llúcia
tracks.title: The cloister — Santa Llúcia, older than the cathedral
tracks.where: At the doorway of the chapel of Santa Llúcia, at a corner of the cloister on the same walk as the Chapter Hall museum; stay at the doorway unless visitors are clearly allowed in.
tracks.what: Santa Llúcia, founded by Bishop Arnau de Gurb, finished 1268 ("thirty years before the Gothic works": our arithmetic, no 1298) (F13.1, S3, S7); part of the bishop's palace, joined to the cathedral from 1431 (F13.3, F13.5, S3 re-read: "part of the Episcopal Palace buildings"); first dedicated to Our Lady and all the holy virgins (F13.2); single nave, slightly pointed barrel vault, "a work of transition" (F13.4); the founder's effigy on a slab over four columns; crozier head and silks, the silks now in Madrid, Granada, Cleveland, New York (F13.9, F13.10); the street-door capitals and "molt mediocre" (F13.6, F13.7, Q11, CA; S3 re-read: on the main portal to Carrer de Santa Llúcia, so not pointed at); 13 December, relics, eyesight (F13.13 DATED, O2); the fair since 1786 (G87, GA2). Audit fixes, 14 Nov 2026: the fair since 1786 cut for length; see notes/AUDIT_FIXES.md.
tracks.listen: A bishop's chapel older than the Gothic cathedral, the silks from his tomb now scattered across two continents, and a blunt verdict on its carving.

tracks.room: The cloister · at the room called Jewish memory, the Old Archive of 1535, its place to be confirmed on site
tracks.title: The cloister · Extra · Jewish memory
tracks.where: In or at the door of the room called Jewish memory, the Old Archive of 1535, with its documents on display; its location must be confirmed on site, and it is not assumed to open off the cloister.
tracks.what: Jewish memory = the Old Archive of 1535: original sales, rentals and wills in Latin, Hebrew and Catalan, "written testimonies that give a voice to the inhabitants of medieval Barcelona" (G101, F15.5, O7, EN); the Call's edge along streets lined by the bishop's properties (G103, re-read: safe wording); a canon leased the land of the smaller Jewish quarter (G106, optional, cut for length); August 1391: preaching that began in Seville, about three hundred dead, survivors converted or fled (G104, GA3; [quietly]); funerary slabs reused as building stone from 1391, the known sites outside the cathedral (G105, GA3, no direction); the chapter's archive here until 1969, about forty thousand parchments, nine papyri in the endpapers of one manuscript (F15.1, F15.2, G102, O9); callback 002 (Almanzor; safe F). Audit fixes, 14 Nov 2026: the Call's edge and the Almanzor callback cut; the room's place is to be confirmed on site (O6); see notes/AUDIT_FIXES.md.
tracks.listen: In the cathedral's old archive, the medieval Jews of Barcelona speak through their contracts and wills, and the year 1391 is remembered plainly.

tracks.room: The Chapter Hall · in front of Bermejo's Pietà
tracks.title: The Chapter Hall — The saint in spectacles
tracks.where: Inside the Chapter Hall museum, in front of the painted panel of the dead Christ across his mother's lap, Bermejo's Pietà; stand back a little so others can see.
tracks.what: Bartolomé Bermejo's Pietà of Canon Desplà, 1490 (F14.2, F14.6, O7, S13); Saint Jerome with reading glasses, reading the Vulgate, lion asleep (F14.5, S14); Desplà kneeling at the right, hat in hand, unshaven (S14 re-read: no beard stated); Desplà canon and archdeacon, humanist, collector of antiquities, rebuilt the archdeacon's house (F14.4, F6.4; self-contained for H, E); the signature in Latin on the frame, 23 April (Q3, F14.3, S14; callback 029 Saint George, safe); Bermejo = Bartolomé de Cárdenas, born in Córdoba, "reddish" (F14.9, S13); "it seems likely that he was a converso" (F14.10, S13, EN); itinerant life (M2); his last known work, death date unknown (F14.11, M2, S14); landscape and foreground (F14.7, M2 EN, S14); London 2019 loan (F14.12) cut for length.
tracks.listen: Bermejo's Pietà: a saint in reading glasses, a tired archdeacon on his knees, a painter's signature, and a landscape full of small living things.

tracks.room: The Chapter Hall · beside the monstrance and the stone font
tracks.title: The Chapter Hall — A throne for the Host
tracks.where: In the Chapter Hall museum, beside the great gilded monstrance on its silver seat, with the stone font with lobed sides nearby; only what is on display is pointed at.
tracks.what: The monstrance, c. 1370–1400 ("the late 1300s"), two tiers, six-sided, gold and gilded silver, pearls and gems, 88 cm; a sapphire and a ruby added while it was being made (G93, GS18; year 1371 cut for the date count); "King Martin's throne": its base since the mid-15th century (O4), in fact a folding bishop's chair of gilded silver with the Barcelona hallmark, the royal link "a late tradition" (F14.16, G94, GS18; tradition, not fact); Corpus 1320, one of the first cities in Christendom (G96; callback 029 safe); the 11th-century lobed font from the Romanesque cathedral (F14.15, F2.8, G92, O7); Huguet's Saint Bernardino and the Guardian Angel, 1465–70 (F14.13, O7); Giuliano di Nofri's terracotta Santa Eulàlia from over the Santa Eulàlia door (F14.14, G92, O7). G97: location conflict, O21 decides (ALT-T). Optional crozier and Lochner relief cut (not confirmed on display; S8 puts the relief in the Sala de Sant Sever). Audit fixes, 14 Nov 2026: the sapphire and ruby cut for length; see notes/AUDIT_FIXES.md.
tracks.listen: A gold monstrance on a silver seat that tradition calls a king's throne, a font from the older cathedral, and the saint who once stood over the door you'll leave by.

tracks.room: The Santa Eulàlia door · just inside the cloister's street door, out of the way
tracks.title: The Santa Eulàlia door — Seventeen centuries on one corner
tracks.where: Just inside the Santa Eulàlia door, the cloister's door to Carrer del Bisbe, standing to one side so people can pass in and out.
tracks.what: Version-neutral recap (H skips 002, 021, 027): more than 1,700 years of history (F1.18, O6 re-read: "history", not "worship") on the corner of the Roman town where the first Christian see stood, the bishops never moved (F1.4, A1); the front finished on her feast day (F5.13; callback 004 safe); Eulàlia, by tradition a girl of thirteen, co-patroness of the cathedral, the archdiocese and the city (F7.3, F7.16, O13); 1936, one clause (F15.7, F15.8 HEDGE; 027 the home); the geese (callback 030 safe); the Santa Eulàlia door, step-free access (ROUTE §1.2 OFF), Bishop Sapera's arms (ROUTE §1.2, SEC-enc); optional, O23: the Pont del Bisbe is 1928 (F6.10, F18.34; cut unless O23 finds it in view); thanks; Carrer del Bisbe just outside (O1).
tracks.listen: The goodbye at the cloister's street door: seventeen centuries on one corner of the Roman town, the girl, the year 1936, the geese, and the way out.
